title: Native Korean Numbers
plainEnglish: The native number set (하나, 둘, 셋…) used to count things, people, animals, age, and the hour.
whenToUse: Use native numbers to count objects, people, and animals, and to say age and o'clock: 사과 세 개 (three apples), 스무 살 (20 years old), 두 시 (two o'clock).
attachmentRule: 1–4 and 20 change shape right before a counter: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무 (한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 마리, 스무 살). From 5 up there is no change: 다섯 개, 열 명. Tens are their own words: 열(10), 스물(20), 서른(30), 마흔(40), 쉰(50), 예순(60), 일흔(70), 여든(80), 아흔(90). Native counting normally stops at 99; from 100 you switch to Sino 백.
contrastWith: Contrast with Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼…), used for minutes, money, and dates. The clock mixes them: the HOUR is native (세 시) but the MINUTE is Sino (삼십 분).

examples.en: My younger sibling is ten years old.
I ordered four cups of coffee.

commonMistakes: Using Sino numbers to count objects — 사과 삼 개 is wrong; say 사과 세 개.
Forgetting the shape change: it is 두 개 (not 둘 개) and 스무 살 (not 스물 살).
beginnerExplanation: Korean has two number systems, and this is the 'native' one. You use it to count things you can see and touch, plus age and the hour on a clock. The tricky part: 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 and 스물 change to 한, 두, 세, 네, 스무 right before a counting word — so 'two cups' is 두 잔, not 둘 잔. From 다섯 (five) on, nothing changes.

title: Sino-Korean Numbers
plainEnglish: The Chinese-derived number set (일, 이, 삼…) used for minutes, money, dates, phone numbers, and large numbers.
whenToUse: Use Sino numbers for minutes (삼십 분), money (천 원), dates (3월 5일), phone numbers, floors, and counting from the hundreds up.
attachmentRule: 일(1) 이(2) 삼(3) 사(4) 오(5) 육(6) 칠(7) 팔(8) 구(9) 십(10), then 백(100), 천(1,000), 만(10,000), 억(100,000,000). Combine the digits: 23 = 이십삼, 105 = 백오, 2024 = 이천이십사. Zero is 영 or 공 (공 in phone numbers). Sino numbers never change shape before a counter.
contrastWith: Contrast with native numbers (하나, 둘…). The classic trap is the clock: the HOUR is native (일곱 시) but the MINUTE is Sino (칠 분), so 7:07 = 일곱 시 칠 분.
commonMistakes: Reading minutes with native numbers — 삼십 분 is right, 서른 분 is wrong.
Forgetting that 6월 and 10월 are read 유월 and 시월 (not 육월/십월).
studyOrder: Learn 백·천·만 and how to combine digits
Apply to money, minutes, and dates
beginnerExplanation: This is the second number system, borrowed from Chinese. You use it for things you measure or label rather than count by hand: money, minutes, dates, phone numbers, and big numbers. Unlike native numbers, these never change shape. Watch the calendar: 6월 is 유월 and 10월 is 시월.

hangul: 한 시 십 분 / 삼월 오일
title: Telling Time & Dates
plainEnglish: How to say clock times and calendar dates — which means mixing the two number systems.
whenToUse: Use when telling the time (두 시 삼십 분 = 2:30) or giving a date (오월 오일 = May 5th, 금요일 = Friday).
attachmentRule: TIME — the hour is a NATIVE number + 시 (한 시, 두 시 … 열두 시); the minute is a SINO number + 분 (오 분, 삼십 분). So 7:15 = 일곱 시 십오 분, and 'half past' is 반 (두 시 반). DATE — year, month, and day all use SINO + 년/월/일: 2024년 3월 5일 = 이천이십사 년 삼 월 오 일. Days of the week use 요일 (월요일, 화요일…). Note the irregular months: 6월 = 유월, 10월 = 시월.
contrastWith: The hour is the ONE everyday time word that uses native numbers; minutes, dates, and years all use Sino. Mixing them up (일곱 분, 칠 시) is the most common beginner mistake.
commonMistakes: Saying 칠 시 (Sino) for 'seven o'clock' — the hour is native: 일곱 시.
Saying 일곱 분 (native) for minutes — minutes are Sino: 칠 분.
studyOrder: Combine them: 일곱 시 칠 분
beginnerExplanation: Telling time in Korean uses BOTH number systems at once, which surprises everyone. The hour is a native number + 시 (일곱 시 = seven o'clock), but the minute is a Sino number + 분 (칠 분 = seven minutes). So 7:07 is 일곱 시 칠 분. Dates are all Sino: 삼월 오일 (March 5). Just remember: hour = native, everything else = Sino.

title: The (으) Insertion Rule
plainEnglish: When a verb/adjective stem ends in a consonant, you add 으 before many endings; vowel-ending stems skip it.
whenToUse: This runs through all of Korean. Whenever an ending is written with (으) — like (으)면, (으)세요, (으)ㄹ 수 있다, (으)러, (으)니까 — you choose the form by the stem's last sound: 먹으면 vs 가면, 먹을 수 있다 vs 갈 수 있다.
attachmentRule: Drop 다 to get the stem. If the stem ends in a VOWEL (no 받침), use the short form: -면, -세요, -ㄹ, -러, -니까, -ㄴ (가면, 가세요, 갈, 가러, 가니까). If the stem ends in a CONSONANT (받침 있음), insert 으: -으면, -으세요, -을, -으러, -으니까, -은 (먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹을, 먹으러, 먹으니까). ㄹ-final stems are special: the ㄹ stays for most endings (살면, 살아요) but DROPS before ㄴ/ㅂ/(으)-endings (살다 → 사세요, 사니까, 산).
contrastWith: It is the SAME choice across many endings, so learn it once instead of memorizing each ending: 갈 거예요 / 먹을 거예요, 가면 / 먹으면, 가세요 / 먹으세요, 가니까 / 먹으니까.
sentenceFrames: (vowel) 가 + 면 → 가면   ·   (consonant) 먹 + 으면 → 먹으면
갈 수 있어요  ·  먹을 수 있어요

examples.en: If you go over there, it's there.
Let's go eat (in order to eat).

commonMistakes: Adding 으 after a vowel stem — 가으면 is wrong; it is 가면.
Forgetting 으 after a consonant stem — 먹면/먹세요 are wrong; it is 먹으면/먹으세요.
studyOrder: Consonant → add 으 (먹으면); vowel → skip it (가면)
beginnerExplanation: This is maybe THE most useful rule in Korean. Many endings are written with (으) in front — like (으)면 'if', (으)세요 'please', (으)ㄹ 수 있다 'can'. The 으 is just a little buffer vowel. If the verb stem ends in a consonant (먹-), add 으: 먹으면, 먹으세요, 먹을 수 있어요. If it ends in a vowel (가-), skip it: 가면, 가세요, 갈 수 있어요. Learn it once and it unlocks dozens of endings at the same time.
